analysis.one_liner: Speeds up 2001 income tax cuts and makes them permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee in the 108th Congress, receiving no hearing or vote after its referral to the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) cut income tax rates, repealed the estate tax gradually, and expanded savings accounts, but every provision was scheduled to expire after 2010 under a Senate budget rule. This bill would have moved the income rate cuts up to 2003 instead of 2006 and repealed the expiration date, making all of the 2001 tax cuts permanent.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income taxpayers benefit most from accelerating and locking in the top rate cut to 35%; heirs of very large estates benefit from making the estate tax repeal permanent; savers benefit from permanent higher limits on retirement and education savings accounts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill moves the individual income tax rate reductions (to 25%, 28%, 33%, and 35%) forward from 2006 to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2002.
It repeals Title IX of the 2001 act — the provision that made every tax cut in that law expire after 2010 to comply with Senate budget rules — thereby making all of the 2001 tax cuts permanent.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the permanent cost of the tax cuts, meaning either larger deficits, reduced government services, or higher taxes on others in later years; the cost is skewed because the largest individual benefits go to top-bracket earners and large estates.

drawbacks.text: Making the 2001 cuts permanent locks in a large, permanent revenue loss, since the sunset provision was designed solely to comply with Senate budget rules rather than as tax policy.

The benefits are concentrated at the top: the rate cuts apply to the highest brackets (33% and 35%), and the 2001 act included a gradual full repeal of the estate tax, which affects only the largest estates.
Permanent tax cuts leave less flexibility to respond to budget pressure; the sunset originally gave Congress a mandatory point to reassess costs versus revenues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Taxpayers at all income levels would have kept lower rates and higher savings limits, but the largest and most permanent gains flow to top earners and large estates, while the full cost lands on the federal budget indefinitely. Because the bill also made every provision of the 2001 law permanent at once, it foreclosed the option of letting expensive or poorly performing provisions lapse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tiberi introduced H.R. 210 on January 7, 2003, the first week of the new Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever recorded on the bill for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and large estates did not lose much from the bill's death, since Congress acted separately in 2003 to accelerate the rate cuts and extend most provisions; the practical effect of this bill dying was that the cuts were not locked in permanently at that time, preserving future Congresses' option to let them expire. It's better understood as a redundant bill that never mattered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — it was redundant and never moved

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and members with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the entire 108th Congress, leaving it to die at referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all recorded support came from Republicans (the sponsor and seven cosponsors), and no recorded opposition exists.

industries.note: The bill would have accelerated the top-bracket cuts (33% and 35%) to 2003 and made them permanent, the provisions whose dollar value is largest for the highest earners. The revenue cost falls on the federal budget, which is borne by everyone.

Making the 2001 act permanent included the scheduled full repeal of the estate tax, a benefit available only to estates large enough to owe it. The bill's death preserved the tax for heirs of the largest fortunes.

The 2001 law raised contribution limits for IRAs, 401(k)-type plans, and education savings accounts; making those permanent would channel more household savings into managed accounts. Savers benefit too, so the industry's interest runs alongside ordinary savers' here.
